sentences.text: Aurorazhdarcho was a relatively small pterosaur with a wingspan of 537.8 mm based on the type specimen.

Fossil impressions indicate that Aurorazhdarcho had an elongated head with a high-positioned eye socket, a snout that may have carried a high, rounded crest, and a relatively short neck with signs of a throat pouch.
The genus is known from a single nearly complete skeleton preserved in three dimensions on a single rock slab, from which the counter-mold was removed, lacking the skull and neck.
It is the oldest known azhdarchoid.

The name comes from the Latin word 'aurora' meaning 'dawn', referring to its antiquity compared to other group members, combined with the genus name Azhdarcho (a mythical Kazakh dragon), and the type species Aurorazhdarcho primordius means 'first' in Latin.

The missing skull and neck elements are visible as impressions because their movement on the lake floor left a natural mold covered by organic remains, and subsequent swelling of the carcass may have caused the head to drift away.
The holotype specimen of Aurorazhdarcho micronyx is considered one of the earliest, if not the very first, documented pterosaur fossils ever found, likely unearthed between 1757 and 1779.
An adult Aurorazhdarcho fossil was uncovered in 1999 by amateur paleontologist Peter Kaszmekat in the Blumenberg Quarry near Eichstätt.

The species Aurorazhdarcho primordius was named and described in 2011 by Eberhard Frey, Christian A. Meyer, and Helmut Tischlinger from the holotype specimen, NMB Sh 110, found in the upper part of the Eichstätt Formation dating to the early Tithonian of the Late Jurassic, approximately 150 million years ago.

Evidence suggests the animal died after a predator attack that nearly ripped off its head and neck, causing the body to sink quickly, and the absence of the head and neck is explained by the animal dying from a partially failed predator attack that nearly tore these parts off.

The holotype individual was likely a subadult male, indicated by fused ischiopubes and the absence of a wide birth canal, while the individual was likely a subadult male, indicated by the fused ischiopubis in the pelvis and the lack of a wide egg-laying canal.
Bennett suggested Aurorazhdarcho's interlocking teeth formed a basket for sieving food, functioning like spoonbill jaws for wading and catching individual prey.

The genus authority is Frey, Meyer & Tischlinger, 2011, the type species is Aurorazhdarcho micronyx, and synonyms include Pterodactylus micronyx von Meyer, 1856 and Aurorazhdarcho primordius Frey et al., 2011.

Originally, describers assigned Aurorazhdarcho to the superfamily Azhdarchoidea and placed it in a new family, Protazhdarchidae, of which it is the only named member, but Bennett in 2013 concluded that the genus is actually a ctenochasmatid based on analysis of specimens attributed to Aurorazhdarcho micronyx, considering its short neck and foot morphology.

Aurorazhdarcho lived during the early Tithonian stage of the Late Jurassic in what is now Bavaria, southern Germany, in the Solnhofen Limestone area of Eichstätt, approximately 150 million years ago, with a time range from 149.2 to 145.06 million years ago.

Bennett concluded that Aurorazhdarcho primordius and Pterodactylus micronyx are the same species, treating primordius as a junior synonym of micronyx, while a 2025 study concluded that both Aurorazhdarcho primordius and Pterodactylus micronyx are junior synonyms of Gnathosaurus subulatus.

Describers rejected cladistic analysis, using comparative methods to find similarity to Ctenochasma elegans but concluding it belonged to Azhdarchoidea due to shared key adaptations, most decisively the low shoulder joint, noting that the position of the shoulder joint in Ctenochasma could not be established, but describers assumed it was high due to the close relationship of that taxon with Pterodactylus.
